facts.fact: Described by Lima & Gerhard in 2001 in Ichthyological Exploration of Freshwaters, vol. 12, no. 2.
The holotype, MZUSP 53989, is from the Rio Pratinha at Fazenda Pratinha, in the municipality of Iraquara, Bahia.
Originally described in Hyphessobrycon, it is now treated as valid as Hasemania negodagua, following Melo et al. 2024.
It is now placed in the family Acestrorhamphidae, not Characidae.
Listed as Hasemania negodagua, with Hyphessobrycon negodagua as a synonym.
The species name refers to the Nego d'água, a legendary man-like creature said to live on river bottoms and attack careless fishermen at night.
The name refers to a legendary man-like creature from central Brazil said to dwell on river bottoms.
Most specimens lack an adipose fin.
It lacks an adipose fin, which separates it from most Hyphessobrycon species.
The body is dark grey, with a black patch toward the rear and white markings on the dorsal and anal fins.
Freshly imported fish that have not yet settled in look silvery.
Its colours are not among the brightest of tetras.
The IUCN Red List assesses it as Near Threatened.
This page gives 2013 as the year of description, which conflicts with the 2001 original description.
Native to northeastern Brazil.
Originally described from specimens collected in the Rio Pratinha, a tributary of the Rio Paraguaçu in Bahia.
Recorded from the upper Paraguaçu River basin in Bahia, Brazil.
The Rio Pratinha feeds the Rio Santo Antônio, which drains into the coastal Rio Paraguaçu.
The Rio Pratinha is a short tributary of the upper Paraguaçu basin, in the Chapada Diamantina in Brazil's semiarid northeast.
Found in freshwater streams with soft, slightly acidic water, sandy bottoms and plenty of fallen twigs and leaves.
The Rio Pratinha has remarkably clear water that emerges from a cave and forms a lagoon.
A freshwater, benthopelagic, tropical fish.
It is a relatively new addition to the aquarium hobby.
Wild-caught fish reach the market only rarely.
Aquarium Glaser has offered it to the wholesale trade.
Tourism has heavily altered the Rio Pratinha in recent decades.
Once abundant in the Rio Pratinha, it is now rarely seen or missing from recent samples.
The video's keepers housed their group in a 400-litre aquarium, where the fish claimed one section of the tank.
Keep it in a group of at least 6, or more if space allows.
The quick-facts table recommends groups of 8 or more.
In the video's tanks, it stayed hardy and thrived even in hard tap water.
Recommended conditions are 23–27 °C, pH 5.5–7.0 and GH 1–12.
An easy feeder.
An omnivore that takes flakes and granules plus live, frozen or freeze-dried foods such as brine shrimp, daphnia, mosquito larvae and bloodworms.
One of the most tightly shoaling tetras, with fish staying only a few centimetres apart.
Peaceful; males' occasional spats are limited to fin flaring and display.
It is suitable for community aquariums.
It uses the bottom to middle levels of the aquarium.
Males make fluttering courtship displays, which led Hans-Georg Evers to call it the 'Butterfly Dwarf Tetra'.
Mature males are deeper and darker in colour, with stronger white edging on the dorsal and anal fins.
Males are slimmer; females are heavier-bodied.
Settled males turn black during courtship, contrasting with white fin edges.
An egg-scatterer; the page notes that specific breeding information is scarce.
Suggested aquarium breeding setup: a dim tank with fine-leaved plants or spawning mops, a mesh bottom, and soft acidic water (pH 5.5–6.5).
According to the page, eggs hatch in about 24–36 hours and fry swim freely about five days later, first eating infusoria.
In breeding terms, it is described as a fairly typical tetra.
